title: Financial Modelling, Lesson 3: the linked three-statement model
subtitle: How the P&L, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement fit together
whyItMatters: The linked three-statement model is the foundation skill of every financial analysis job, and the most common test in an industry interview. Understanding the links that make the three statements tie is understanding how accounting actually works in practice.
openingQuestion: In a three-statement model, what proves your model is right?
openingOptions: Net profit is positive in every forecast year
The balance sheet ties: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Operating cash flow always runs higher than reported net profit
explanation: A balance sheet that ties is the automatic check on a three-statement model. If every link is wired correctly - net profit flowing into retained earnings, depreciation added back in the cash flow, working capital changes carried through with the right sign - the balance sheet ties by itself. Out by even one dong means a link is wired wrong.

diagram.label: → CF: add back depreciation, ± working capital
→ Closing cash (BS) → the balance sheet ties

realWorldExample.description: The most common interview question in finance: 'Depreciation rises by 10 - what happens across the three statements?' The answer: P&L - expense up 10, pre-tax profit down 10, tax down 2 (at a 20% rate), net profit down 8. CF - start from net profit at −8, add back depreciation of +10, cash up 2. BS - cash up 2, fixed assets down 10, total assets down 8; retained earnings down 8. Both sides tie.

quiz.question: Which line does net profit from the P&L flow into on the balance sheet?
options: Cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet
Retained earnings on the balance sheet
Paid-in capital contributed by the owners
Long-term borrowings owed to the lending bank
quiz.explanation: Closing retained earnings = opening retained earnings + net profit − dividends. This is the main link joining the P&L to the balance sheet. Net profit does not flow straight into cash, because a large part of it may sit in receivables or inventory rather than the bank. Paid-in capital only changes when shareholders put money in or shares are bought back, which is a financing event rather than an earnings one. And borrowings move when the company draws down or repays a loan, entirely independently of whether the year was profitable.

quiz.question: Why is depreciation added back in the cash flow statement?
options: It is an accounting rule with no particular reason
Because depreciation raises the carrying value of the asset
Because it is an expense that never leaves the company as cash
Because it is income that was left out when the accounts were drawn
quiz.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense. Operating cash flow starts from net profit, so anything deducted on the way to net profit that did not actually consume cash has to be added back. There is a clear reason for it, so it is not an arbitrary convention. Depreciation reduces the carrying value of the asset rather than raising it - that is the whole point of the charge. And it is an expense, not income that was somehow omitted; the cash was spent years earlier when the asset was bought.

quiz.question: How does a 50bn increase in receivables during the period affect cash flow?
options: Cash flow rises by 50bn because revenue rose in the period
Cash flow rises by 50bn but accounting profit falls
No effect, since this is only a balance sheet item
Cash flow falls by 50bn because the cash sits with customers
quiz.explanation: The revenue has already been recognised on the P&L but the money has not arrived. A rise in current assets is a fall in cash flow - which is exactly why a fast-growing company can still run out of money. Growing receivables cannot raise cash, since by definition the customer has not paid. The profit figure is unaffected, because revenue was booked at invoice. And treating it as a balance-sheet-only item ignores the entire purpose of the working capital section of the cash flow statement.

quiz.question: What is the final link that closes a three-statement model?
options: Closing cash on the cash flow statement into the balance sheet
Revenue from the income statement carried across to the balance sheet
Interest expense taken straight into closing shareholders' equity
Depreciation for the period added into net revenue
quiz.explanation: The closing cash balance from the cash flow statement is the cash line on the balance sheet. Once that link is wired, the balance sheet ties by itself provided everything else is right. Revenue never appears on the balance sheet at all; it reaches equity only after passing through net profit. Interest expense also runs through the P&L rather than being posted straight to equity. And depreciation is a cost, so adding it into revenue would inflate the top line with something that was never a sale.

quiz.question: The balance sheet in your model is out by a small amount. What is the most efficient way to find the error?
options: Recheck every formula in all three statements from the first year to the last
Find the first year that breaks, then inspect that year's links alone
Add the difference to an adjustment line so the balance sheet ties
Rebuild the balance sheet from scratch, since link errors are rarely found
quiz.explanation: A linking error propagates into every year after it, so the first year that breaks is where the real fault lies. What you check there is the three familiar links: profit into retained earnings, depreciation added back, and the change in working capital. Rechecking everything is enormously slower and no more reliable. Plugging the difference hides the error rather than fixing it, and the hidden error will distort every output you build on the model. And rebuilding from scratch usually just reproduces the same mistake.

keyTakeaways: Three core links: NI → retained earnings; depreciation added back in CF; closing cash in CF → cash on the BS
A balance sheet that ties is the automatic check - out of balance means a link is wrong
Current assets up = cash flow down; payables up = cash flow up
Never 'force' the balance sheet to tie with a manual adjustment - go and find the real error

practicePrompt.question: Your model shows the balance sheet out by exactly 200bn in every forecast year, with the gap unchanged across periods. What is the most likely cause?
options: One line item was linked wrongly in the very first period
The tax rate was entered incorrectly in the model
The forecast revenue figures are far too high
Add a further 200bn adjustment line to bring it back into balance
practicePrompt.explanation: A gap that stays CONSTANT across every period is the classic signature of an error in the opening period - usually a balance sheet line omitted at the start, with the error then carried forward. A gap that grows over time is normally a fault in a recurring flow instead. Never add an adjustment line to force it to tie: that hides the error rather than fixing it.

summary.keyIdea: Three statements joined by three links; a balance sheet that ties is the proof they are wired correctly
summary.formula: Closing retained earnings = opening + Net profit − Dividends
summary.commonMistake: Adding a plug line to force the balance sheet to tie, hiding the real error underneath.
summary.action: Answer the classic interview question for yourself: depreciation rises by 10 - what changes across the three statements?

application.title: Test yourself with the depreciation question
application.message: You do not need Excel: take a pen and paper, assume depreciation rises by 10 with a 20% tax rate, and write out the change on all three statements. If both sides of the balance sheet tie, you have the linking mechanism.
application.secondary: This is the single most widely used test in financial analysis interviews.

sections.text: The three-statement model is where accounting comes alive: you watch a business decision run through profit, settle on the balance sheet and finally turn into cash - or fail to.
The three links joining the three statements

items: **P&L → Balance sheet:** net profit adds to retained earnings (after dividends are deducted)
**P&L → Cash flow:** start from net profit and add back non-cash charges such as depreciation
**Cash flow → Balance sheet:** the closing cash balance becomes the cash line on the balance sheet

example.title: Depreciation rises by 10, at a 20% tax rate
example.calculation: P&L: expense +10 → pre-tax profit −10 → tax −2 → net profit −8  ||  CF: −8 (net profit) +10 (depreciation added back) = +2 cash  ||  BS: cash +2, fixed assets −10 → total assets −8; retained earnings −8
example.result: Both sides fall by 8 - the balance sheet still ties
example.explanation: This is the classic interview question. Answering it fluently means you have the linking mechanism, not just a memorised formula.

sections.label: Never force it to tie
sections.text: When the balance sheet is out, the great temptation is to add an adjustment line to close the gap. Don't. The size of the gap is the most valuable information you have: a constant gap across periods is usually an error in the opening period; a growing gap is usually an error in a recurring flow.

sections.title: Sign conventions in the cash flow statement

concepts.def: Cash flow DOWN - the money is tied up in inventory or receivables
Cash flow UP - you are financing yourself on your suppliers' money
Added back to operating cash flow (depreciation, amortisation)
A line added to force the balance sheet to tie - the sign of an error you have not found yet

lines: A balance sheet that ties is not the goal - it is the evidence you wired it correctly.
